cards.front: Recall a key point about Crowd & Collective Behaviour
cards.back: Deindividuation: losing your sense of personal identity in a crowd, which can lead to behaviour you would not normally do. Anonymity (e.g. uniforms, masks) reduces self-awareness and increases conformity to group norms.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Crowd & Collective Behaviour
cards.back: Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner): we derive part of our identity from group membership. Process: social categorisation -> social identification -> social comparison. This can lead to in-group favouritism and out-group discrimination.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Crowd & Collective Behaviour
cards.back: Tajfel's minimal group paradigm: even when groups are assigned arbitrarily (e.g. preference for Klee vs Kandinsky), participants favoured their in-group. This shows that even meaningless group distinctions create bias.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Crowd & Collective Behaviour
cards.back: Prejudice: a negative attitude towards a group based on stereotypes. Discrimination: unfair treatment based on group membership. Causes: social identity, scapegoating, media representations, and authoritarian personality.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Crowd & Collective Behaviour
cards.back: Reducing prejudice: intergroup contact (Allport's contact hypothesis), superordinate goals (Sherif's Robbers Cave experiment), and education about stereotyping.

cards.front: What should you know about psychology exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating crowd behaviour and prejudice, consider: lab vs real-world, cultural factors, and practical applications (how can findings reduce discrimination in schools and workplaces?).

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Crowds always make people behave more aggressively than they would alone. Correct: Deindividuation theory shows that crowds lead people to follow group norms - which can be aggressive or prosocial.
